title: Instructional Fidelity: The Price of Certainty
author: Terry Underwood, PhD
source: Learning to Read, Reading to Learn, May 22, 2026
summary: Terry Underwood argues that scripted phonics programs are not primarily pedagogical tools but political artifacts -- fidelity-delivery mechanisms engineered to make teachers interchangeable and give legislators the appearance of having solved the reading problem. He traces the consolidation of an evidence regime from the 2000 National Reading Panel through state-by-state science-of-reading legislation, showing how each stage tightened the fidelity loop and narrowed what counts as legitimate evidence. Two proven teacher-centered interventions -- Reading Recovery and Reciprocal Teaching -- are examined as evidence that judgment-dependent methods work but have been stalled or restricted, not because their evidence was bad, but because it violated design standards built for phonemic awareness trials rather than dialogic classroom practice. The 158 Reciprocal Teaching studies the WWC excluded are dissected: disqualifying criteria systematically rejected studies on underserved students -- the exact populations the interventions were designed to reach. Underwood draws the medical analogy: physicians treat guidelines as a floor from which to deviate when the patient warrants it; scripted phonics treats evidence as a ceiling, and the teacher who responds to the child in front of her becomes the contaminating variable. The cost is borne by the six-year-old already falling behind and the adolescent who reads fluently but cannot make meaning from a complex page.
points: Scripted phonics functions as a political artifact -- a device for declaring the reading problem solved -- more than an evidence-based pedagogical tool.
Reading Recovery and Reciprocal Teaching both earned WWC acknowledgment of efficacy yet have been restricted by state legislatures acting on that same regime's approval structure.
The WWC excluded 158 of 164 Reciprocal Teaching studies, with criteria that systematically disqualified studies on underserved students -- precisely the children the interventions targeted.
The fidelity-to-protocol model treats teacher judgment as contamination, inverting the medical model where clinical deviation from a guideline is expected when the patient warrants it.

The script persists because training a workforce for the clinical judgment required by adaptive interventions demands massive, ongoing structural investment that institutions chronically refuse to make.
quotes: Scripted phonics is what you get when an evidence regime that demands fidelity to a protocol meets a political body that demands certainty, peace of mind. This has nothing to do with science; science rejects certainty and demands falsifiability. The script isn't primarily a pedagogical artifact. It is a fidelity-delivery mechanism.

A mandated curriculum or a scripted program allows politicians to declare they have 'solved' the problem without having to do the targeted work of training and supporting teachers as professional learners and practitioners or addressing underlying inequities.

Teachers pay a severe cost for second-hand certainty: their authority to interpret empirical research for themselves is denied, and their license to respond to the complexities of the classroom is revoked. Medical researchers do not write protocols that interchangeable practitioners read verbatim. They write guidelines that credentialed clinicians interpret in light of the patient and the patient's circumstances.

Scripts and fidelity protocols are written for substitute teachers. Deviation is reframed as infidelity and used to invalidate the intervention's effect. The teacher who reads the child in front of them is, by the regime's own grammar, the contaminating variable.

Medicine uses evidence as a floor for practice. Most children do need phonics instruction to varying degrees in particular contexts. That's a floor. Scripted phonics uses evidence as a ceiling. Fidelity is the price of feeling certain. Judgment is the price of being relevant.

The cost is paid by the six-year-old who is already feeling and falling behind, and by the songbird in seventh-grade English who loves to read series books and has not yet been taught what to do with a page that resists easy resolution.
